blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 4 (Stoichiometry), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Define the mole and Avogadro's number. Explain with examples that one mole of atoms, molecules, formula units and ions contains the same number of particles, and show how the molar mass of CCl₄ is found. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Mole: the amount of a substance which contains as many elementary entities as there are atoms in 0.012 kg (12 g) of carbon-12. The entities may be atoms, molecules, ions, electrons or other particles. It is represented by n.

Avogadro's number: the number of entities present in one mole of a substance is a constant, 6.02 × 10²³, represented by Nₐ (after the Italian scientist Amedeo Avogadro, 1776-1856).

Examples:
• 1 mole of ¹²C contains 6.02 × 10²³ atoms of ¹²C.
• 1 mole of H₂O contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules of H₂O.
• 1 mole of NaCl contains 6.02 × 10²³ formula units of NaCl.
• 1 mole of Na⁺ contains 6.02 × 10²³ ions of Na⁺.
Chemists use the mole as the SI unit to weigh and count atoms, molecules, formula units or ions.

Molar mass: the mass of one mole of a substance expressed in grams (unit g/mol). It is the sum of the masses of the component atoms:
Molar mass of CCl₄ = 12.0 × 1 + 35.5 × 4 = 12.0 + 142.0 = 154.0 g/mol.

book_ref.quote: The number of entities present in one mole of a substance is a constant number named Avogadro

blocks.prompt: 2 Calculate (i) the number of moles in 31.6 g of CaO (molar mass 56.1 g mol⁻¹) and (ii) the mass of 0.150 mol of Na₂CO₃ (molar mass 106 g mol⁻¹). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use n = m/M to get moles from mass, and m = n × M to get mass from moles.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the mass of 10⁻³ mol of MgSO₄

steps: (ii) m = n × M = 0.150 mol × 106 g mol⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: (i) 0.563 mol of CaO; (ii) 15.9 g of Na₂CO₃

blocks.prompt: 3 Explain the relationship between mole, molar mass and Avogadro's number for elements, compounds and ions, with examples. Write the formulas connecting mass, moles and number of particles. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Elements: different masses of elements have the same number of atoms when each is one mole. 12.0 g of carbon and 4.0 g of helium each contain 6.02 × 10²³ atoms.
1.0 g of hydrogen = 1 mol of H = 6.02 × 10²³ atoms
23.0 g of sodium = 1 mol of Na = 6.02 × 10²³ atoms
238.0 g of uranium = 1 mol of U = 6.02 × 10²³ atoms
A sodium atom is 23 times heavier than a hydrogen atom, so to have equal numbers of atoms sodium must be taken 23 times greater in mass.

Compounds: one mole of different compounds has different masses but the same number of molecules.
18.0 g of H₂O = 1 mol = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules; 180.0 g of glucose = 1 mol = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules.

Ions: the number of ions in one mole of any ionic species is Avogadro's number.
96.1 g of SO₄²⁻ = 1 mol = 6.02 × 10²³ ions; 62.0 g of NO₃⁻ = 1 mol = 6.02 × 10²³ ions.

Formulas:
Number of moles = mass / molar mass
Number of moles = number of particles / Nₐ
Number of particles = mass × Nₐ / molar mass

book_ref.quote: A sample of 12.0 grams of natural carbon contains the same number of atoms as 4.0 grams of natural helium

blocks.prompt: 4 A cylinder contains 7.1 g of chlorine gas, Cl₂ (molar mass 71.0 g mol⁻¹). Calculate (i) the moles of Cl₂, (ii) the number of Cl₂ molecules, (iii) the number of chlorine atoms and (iv) its volume at STP. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Mass → moles (÷ M); moles → molecules (× Nₐ); each Cl₂ has 2 atoms; moles → volume (× 22.4 dm³).

book_ref.quote: Number of moles of sodium = 2.3/23.0 = 0.1 mol

blocks.final_answer: 0.10 mol; 6.02 × 10²² molecules; 1.204 × 10²³ Cl atoms; 2.24 dm³ at STP

blocks.prompt: 5 A bee releases about 1 μg (1 × 10⁻⁶ g) of isopentyl acetate, C₇H₁₄O₂, when it stings. (i) Calculate the molar mass of C₇H₁₄O₂ (C = 12.0, H = 1.0, O = 16.0). (ii) How many moles and how many molecules are released? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Add the atomic masses to get M, then n = m/M and molecules = n × Nₐ.

book_ref.quote: Isopentyl acetate (C₇H₁₄O₂) is the compound responsible for the scent of bananas

blocks.prompt: 6 What is molar volume? State Avogadro's law and explain how 22.4 dm³ of a gas at STP is related to its molar mass, Avogadro's number and one mole, with examples. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Molar volume: the volume of one mole of an ideal gas at STP. Its value is 22.414 dm³, commonly rounded to 22.4 dm³, and it is denoted by Vₘ. With it, the mass or moles of a gas at STP can be converted into volume, and vice versa.

Avogadro's law: equal volumes of all ideal gases at the same temperature and pressure contain equal numbers of molecules.

This means one mole of an ideal gas at STP (273.15 K and 1 atm) has a volume of 22.414 dm³. Since one mole of a gas has Avogadro's number of particles, 22.4 dm³ of every ideal gas at STP contains 6.02 × 10²³ molecules:
22.4 dm³ of a gas at STP = molar mass of the gas = 6.02 × 10²³ particles = 1 mole
• 22.4 dm³ of CO₂ = 44.0 g = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules = 1 mole
• 22.4 dm³ of H₂ = 2 g = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules = 1 mole
• 22.4 dm³ of NH₃ = 17 g = 6.02 × 10²³ molecules = 1 mole

Volume from moles: V = n × Vₘ.

book_ref.quote: Since one mole of a gas has Avogadro’s number of particles

blocks.prompt: 7 A gas has a density of 2.86 g dm⁻³ at STP. Calculate (i) its molar mass and (ii) the volume occupied by 16.0 g of this gas at STP. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: One mole occupies 22.4 dm³ at STP, so molar mass = density × 22.4; then moles = mass/M and V = n × 22.4.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the molar mass of a gas which has density of 1.97 g/dm³ at STP

steps: (i) m = d × V = 2.86 g dm⁻³ × 22.4 dm³ mol⁻¹
blocks.final_answer: Molar mass 64.1 g mol⁻¹; 16.0 g occupies 5.59 dm³ at STP

blocks.prompt: 8 Define density and molar concentration. Explain why the density of a gas at STP depends on its molar mass, and describe how the number of moles is found from mass, particles, gas volume and molar concentration. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Density: the mass per unit volume of a substance, d = m/V.
All gases have the same molar volume (22.4 dm³) at STP, so the density of a gas depends on its molar mass: a gas of higher molar mass has a higher density, and vice versa. If the density at STP is measured, the molar mass = d × 22.4.

Molar concentration: the number of moles of a substance (reactant or product) dissolved per dm³ of solution, unit mol/dm³:
C = n/V and n = C × V, where V is the volume of the solution in dm³.

Number of moles (concept map):
• from mass: n = mass / molar mass
• from particles: n = number of particles / Nₐ
• from gas volume at STP: n = V / 22.4 dm³
• from a solution: n = C × V

book_ref.quote: which is the number of moles of a substance (reactant or product) dissolved per volume of a solution in dm³

blocks.prompt: 9 6.91 g of K₂CO₃ (molar mass 138.2 g mol⁻¹) is dissolved in water to make 250 cm³ of solution. (i) Calculate the molar concentration. (ii) What mass of K₂CO₃ would be needed to make 500 cm³ of a 0.100 mol dm⁻³ solution? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Change cm³ to dm³ (÷ 1000), then C = n/V; for (ii) n = C × V and m = n × M.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the molar concentration of a substance containing 27.64 g of K₂CO₃

steps: (ii) n = C × V = 0.100 mol dm⁻³ × 0.500 dm³ = 0.0500 mol

blocks.prompt: 10 What is stoichiometry? Interpret the balanced equation N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) in terms of moles, molecules, volumes and masses, and name the stoichiometric relationships it allows. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Stoichiometry: the branch of chemistry which tells us the quantitative relationship between reactants and products in a balanced chemical equation. Using mole, Avogadro's number, molar mass, molar volume and molar concentration, these relationships are worked out.

N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g) can be read in four ways:
• Moles: 1 mole of N₂ reacts with 3 moles of H₂ to form 2 moles of NH₃.
• Molecules: 1 molecule of N₂ reacts with 3 molecules of H₂ to form 2 molecules of NH₃.
• Volumes (STP): 22.4 dm³ of N₂ reacts with 67.2 dm³ of H₂ to form 44.8 dm³ of NH₃.
• Masses: 28.0 g of N₂ reacts with 6 g of H₂ to form 34.0 g of NH₃ (28.0 + 6 = 34.0, mass is conserved).

Relationships: mole-mole, mass-mass, volume-volume, mole-mass, mole-volume and mass-volume.

Assumptions: all reactants are completely converted into products; the laws of conservation of mass and definite proportions are obeyed; no side reaction occurs.

book_ref.quote: To understand these relationships, we need to interpret information hidden in a balanced chemical equation

blocks.prompt: 11 In the reaction 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s), 50.0 g of Fe₂O₃ (159.6 g mol⁻¹) reacts completely. Calculate (i) the mass of Al (27 g mol⁻¹) needed and (ii) the mass of Fe (55.8 g mol⁻¹) formed. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Mass-mass: mass of Fe₂O₃ → moles, use the mole ratio Fe₂O₃ : Al : Fe = 1 : 2 : 2, then moles → mass.

book_ref.quote: From the balanced equation, 1 mol of Fe₂O₃ reacts with 2 moles of Al

blocks.final_answer: (i) 16.9 g of Al; (ii) 35.0 g of Fe

blocks.prompt: 12 30.0 dm³ of N₂ at STP reacts with excess H₂: N₂(g) + 3H₂(g) → 2NH₃(g). Calculate (i) the volume of H₂ used, (ii) the volume of NH₃ formed and (iii) the mass of NH₃ formed (17.0 g mol⁻¹). (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: For gases at STP the volume ratio is the mole ratio (1 : 3 : 2); then moles of NH₃ = V/22.4 and mass = n × M.

book_ref.quote: So, the volume of ammonia produced by the reaction of 100 dm³ of H₂ with excess nitrogen is 66.7 dm³

blocks.final_answer: 90.0 dm³ of H₂; 60.0 dm³ of NH₃; 45.5 g of NH₃

blocks.prompt: 13 In a space vehicle, LiOH removes exhaled CO₂: 2LiOH(s) + CO₂(g) → Li₂CO₃(s) + H₂O(l). Calculate the mass of LiOH (23.9 g mol⁻¹) needed to absorb 11.0 g of CO₂ (44.0 g mol⁻¹), and the mass of Li₂CO₃ (73.9 g mol⁻¹) formed. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Mass of CO₂ → moles; ratio LiOH : CO₂ : Li₂CO₃ = 2 : 1 : 1; moles → mass.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the mass of Li₂CO₃ that can be produced by 20.0 mol of LiOH

blocks.final_answer: 12.0 g of LiOH needed; 18.5 g of Li₂CO₃ formed

blocks.prompt: 14 8.37 g of iron (55.8 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess sulphuric acid: Fe(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → FeSO₄(aq) + H₂(g). Calculate (i) the moles of H₂SO₄ used, (ii) the volume of H₂ at STP and (iii) the number of H₂ molecules formed. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Mass-volume: moles of Fe; ratio Fe : H₂SO₄ : H₂ = 1 : 1 : 1; then V = n × 22.4 and molecules = n × Nₐ.

book_ref.quote: Number of moles of iron (n) = m/M = 7.0 g / 55.8 gmol⁻¹ = 0.125 mol

blocks.final_answer: 0.150 mol of H₂SO₄; 3.36 dm³ of H₂; 9.03 × 10²² molecules

blocks.prompt: 15 What are limiting and excess reactants? Why is an inexpensive reactant often supplied in excess? Explain with the reaction of hydrogen and oxygen. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
In many processes the reactants are not present in the proportions of the balanced equation. A large amount of the inexpensive reactant is often supplied:
• to ensure the whole of the expensive reactant is completely converted to the desired product;
• to produce the maximum amount of product;
• to increase the rate of reaction.
For example, a large quantity of oxygen makes things burn more rapidly; excess oxygen is left and the fuel is consumed earlier.

Limiting reactant: the reactant which controls the amounts of products formed and is consumed earlier. Once it is consumed, the reaction stops and no more product forms; the maximum product depends on its amount.
Excess (non-limiting) reactant: the reactant left unreacted after the completion of reaction.

Example: 2H₂(g) + O₂(g) → 2H₂O(l)
• 2 moles of H₂ (4 g) with 2 moles of O₂ (64 g): 2 moles of H₂ react with only 1 mole (32 g) of O₂, giving 2 moles (36 g) of water. H₂ is limiting; 1 mole of O₂ is left in excess.
• 1 mole of H₂ with 1 mole of O₂: 1 mole of H₂ needs ½ mole of O₂, so all H₂ reacts and ½ mole of O₂ is left in excess.

book_ref.quote: The reactant which controls the amounts of products formed in a chemical reaction and is consumed earlier

blocks.prompt: 16 Describe the strategy (steps) for identifying the limiting reactant. How does smothering a fire use the idea of an excess reactant? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Steps to identify the limiting reactant:
1. Calculate the number of moles from the given amounts of reactants.
2. Find the number of moles of product from each reactant with the help of the balanced chemical equation.
3. The reactant which produces the least amount of product is the limiting reactant; the other is the excess reactant.
Then the maximum product is found from the limiting reactant, and the excess left = amount taken − amount used.

Smothering: fire is a combustion reaction in which fuel and oxygen combine, usually at high temperatures, to form water and carbon dioxide. Once started it is self-supporting. Smothering reduces the available oxygen below the level needed to support combustion, i.e. it decreases the amount of the excess reactant, so the fire stops. Foams, inert gas and CO₂ are effective substances for smothering.

book_ref.quote: Identify the reactant which produces the least amount of product as limiting reactant and the other as an excess reactant

blocks.prompt: 17 3.40 g of NH₃ (17.0 g mol⁻¹) is heated with 31.8 g of CuO (79.5 g mol⁻¹): 2NH₃(g) + 3CuO(s) → N₂(g) + 3Cu(s) + 3H₂O(g). (i) Identify the limiting reactant. (ii) Calculate the mass of N₂ (28.0 g mol⁻¹) formed. (iii) Find the mass of excess reactant left. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Find moles of each reactant, then moles of N₂ each could give; the smaller decides. Use the molar mass of N₂, not NH₃.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the mass of N₂ produced from 1.81 g of NH₃

steps: N₂ from NH₃ = 1/2 × 0.200 = 0.100 mol; N₂ from CuO = 1/3 × 0.400 = 0.133 mol
(i) NH₃ gives less N₂, so NH₃ is the limiting reactant
blocks.final_answer: NH₃ is limiting; 2.80 g of N₂; 7.95 g of CuO left

blocks.prompt: 18 0.400 dm³ of 0.100 mol dm⁻³ Pb(NO₃)₂ is mixed with 0.300 dm³ of 0.200 mol dm⁻³ Na₂SO₄: Na₂SO₄(aq) + Pb(NO₃)₂(aq) → PbSO₄(s) + 2NaNO₃(aq). Find the limiting ion, the mass of PbSO₄ (303.3 g mol⁻¹) precipitated and the moles of the ion left in excess. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Use n = C × V for each ion; Pb²⁺ + SO₄²⁻ → PbSO₄ is 1 : 1, so the smaller amount is limiting.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the mass of PbSO₄ formed when 1.25 dm³ of 0.05 mol dm⁻³ Pb(NO₃)₂

steps: Ratio 1 : 1, so Pb²⁺ (0.0400 mol) is limiting; PbSO₄ formed = 0.0400 mol
blocks.final_answer: Pb²⁺ is limiting; 12.1 g of PbSO₄; 0.0200 mol of SO₄²⁻ left

blocks.prompt: 19 24.0 g of CH₄ (16.0 g mol⁻¹) is burnt with 80.0 g of O₂ (32.0 g mol⁻¹): CH₄(g) + 2O₂(g) → CO₂(g) + 2H₂O(g). (i) Which is the limiting reactant? (ii) What mass of CO₂ (44.0 g mol⁻¹) forms? (iii) What mass of excess reagent is left unreacted? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Follow the steps: moles of each reactant, moles of CO₂ from each, the smaller is from the limiting reactant, then excess left = taken − used.

book_ref.quote: How many grams of CO₂ can be produced when 30 g of CH₄ and 50 g of O₂ are allowed to combine

steps: CO₂ from CH₄ = 1.50 mol; CO₂ from O₂ = 1/2 × 2.50 = 1.25 mol
(i) O₂ gives less CO₂, so O₂ is the limiting reactant
blocks.final_answer: O₂ is limiting; 55.0 g of CO₂; 4.0 g of CH₄ left

blocks.prompt: 20 Define actual yield, theoretical yield and percentage yield. Explain the reasons for which the amount of product obtained in most reactions is less than expected, and state how % yield shows efficiency. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Actual yield: the amount of product actually obtained in a chemical reaction.
Theoretical yield: the amount of product calculated from the balanced chemical equation; it is the maximum amount of product that can be produced by a given amount of reactant.

Reasons why the actual yield is usually less:
1. Processes like filtration, separation by distillation or a separating funnel, washing, drying and crystallization, if not properly carried out, decrease the actual yield.
2. Some of the reactants might take part in a competing side reaction and reduce the amount of the desired product.
3. A reaction may be reversible, so the amount of product is reduced by the backward reaction.

Percentage yield: the efficiency of a reaction is expressed by comparing the actual and theoretical yields as a percentage:
% yield = (actual yield / theoretical yield) × 100
The greater the percentage yield, the higher the efficiency of the reaction, and vice versa.

book_ref.quote: In most chemical reactions the amount of the product obtained is less than the theoretical yield

blocks.prompt: 21 Aspirin is prepared by heating 5.00 g of salicylic acid, C₇H₆O₃ (138.12 g mol⁻¹), with 5.00 g of acetic anhydride, C₄H₆O₃ (102.09 g mol⁻¹): C₇H₆O₃ + C₄H₆O₃ → C₉H₈O₄ + CH₃COOH. (i) Find the limiting reactant. (ii) Calculate the theoretical yield of aspirin (180.16 g mol⁻¹). (iii) Find the % yield if 5.20 g of aspirin is obtained. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: All ratios are 1 : 1, so the reactant with fewer moles is limiting; it fixes the theoretical yield; then % yield = actual/theoretical × 100.

book_ref.quote: Calculate the theoretical yield of aspirin, (molar mass 180.16 gmol⁻¹)

steps: n(salicylic acid) = 5.00 / 138.12 = 0.0362 mol; n(acetic anhydride) = 5.00 / 102.09 = 0.0490 mol
(i) Salicylic acid has fewer moles, so it is the limiting reactant
blocks.final_answer: Salicylic acid is limiting; theoretical yield 6.52 g; 79.7 % yield

blocks.prompt: 22 10.0 g of aluminium (27 g mol⁻¹) reacts with excess Fe₂O₃: 2Al(s) + Fe₂O₃(s) → Al₂O₃(s) + 2Fe(s). If 18.0 g of iron (55.8 g mol⁻¹) is actually obtained, calculate the theoretical yield of iron and the percentage yield. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Al is the limiting reactant (Fe₂O₃ is in excess); Al : Fe = 2 : 2 = 1 : 1 gives the theoretical yield.

book_ref.quote: The amount of the products calculated from the balanced chemical equation represents the theoretical yield

steps: Theoretical yield of Fe = 0.3704 × 55.8 = 20.67 g ≈ 20.7 g
blocks.final_answer: Theoretical yield 20.7 g of Fe; 87.1 % yield

blocks.prompt: 23 Explain the importance of stoichiometry in the production and dosage of medicines, and describe its uses in the field of medicine. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Production and dosage: while preparing a dose of a medicine, the optimum amount of the active ingredient is essential to produce the desired effect in the patient. Stoichiometry ensures the accuracy of drug synthesis; any deviation can result in incomplete reaction or contamination with unreacted reactants or by-products. It allows chemists to precisely control reactions to produce drugs and ensure their efficiency, effectiveness and safe use.

Uses in medicine:
• Antibiotics: stoichiometry ensures that each dose matches the active ingredient and target bacteria.
• Cholesterol: to determine the cholesterol level in the blood of patients (cholesterol is a form of fat that is not all bad but can have harmful effects).
• Glucose: to determine the glucose level in the blood of a diabetic patient; use of insulin relies on stoichiometry for precise control of blood sugar.
• Athletes: to determine steroids and other stimulants in the urine of athletes.
• Vaccines: to determine the concentration of viral antigens for effective results.
• Dosage: to determine the amount of drug for a patient. A medicine has no effect in small amounts and can cause a toxic state or death in large amounts; e.g. an overdose of paracetamol (a pain killer and fever reducer) may cause organ damage and severe liver damage.

book_ref.quote: Stoichiometry allows chemists to precisely control chemical reactions to produce drugs
